title: Episode 211: The Roman Empire: The Destruction of Jerusalem: Masada, Titus, and the Arch of Rome
description:
In 66 AD, seven decades of simmering Jewish resentment against corrupt Roman procurators, heavy taxation, and religious insults erupted into the Great Jewish Revolt. Expelling the Roman garrison from Jerusalem and annihilating the Twelfth Legion in the Pass of Beth Horon, Jewish Zealots declared total national independence. In response, Emperor Nero dispatched Rome's most seasoned general, Vespasian, and his son Titus with four veteran legions to execute a systematic campaign of subjugation. Following the bloody conquest of Galilee, Titus laid a suffocating five-month siege to Jerusalem in 70 AD, constructing a five-mile siege wall around the holy city. As internal civil war and catastrophic famine devastated the defenders, Roman battering rams breached the three walls of Jerusalem. In August 70 AD, the Second Temple was consumed by an apocalyptic inferno and leveled to its foundations. Discover the tragic fall of Zion, the final stand atop the desert fortress of Masada, and the triumphal Arch of Titus in the Roman Forum.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our twelve-part Great Biblical Empires saga with one of the most cataclysmic sieges in the history of warfare: The Destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD. In the clash between Jewish zeal and Roman iron, an ancient world vanished in smoke and stone. Here is George with the story of Titus, the burning of the Temple, and the rock of Masada.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SPARK OF 66 AD: THE GREAT REVOLT
Following the death of Herod the Great, Judea was ruled directly by a succession of corrupt, greedy Roman procurators who plundered the province and insulted Jewish religious sensibilities. In May 66 AD, procurator Gessius Florus seized seventeen talents of gold from the Temple treasury, provoking public protests. When mocking youths passed around a collection basket for the 'poor procurator,' Florus unleashed his auxiliary troops on the Upper Market, crucifying three thousand six hundred Jewish citizens, including Roman citizens of equestrian rank. The outrage ignited a long-smoldering fire: Eleazar ben Hanania, captain of the Temple guard, ceased the daily sacrifices offered on behalf of the Roman Emperor, marking an official declaration of rebellion. Zealot factions seized the Antonia Fortress, slaughtering the Roman garrison. When Cestius Gallus, Roman governor of Syria, marched south with the Twelfth Legion 'Fulminata' to restore order, Jewish fighters ambushed the legions in the narrow gorge of the Beth Horon Pass, annihilating six thousand Roman soldiers and capturing their eagle standards and siege engines. The Great Jewish Revolt had begun. The Great Jewish Revolt of 66 AD was ignited by decades of Roman procuratorial cruelty, corruption, and religious desecration. The initial defeat of the Twelfth Legion at Beth Horon gave the Zealots a false sense that divine intervention would grant them victory over Rome.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: VESPASIAN AND THE SUBJUGATION OF GALILEE
Shocked by the humiliating loss of an entire legion, Emperor Nero appointed Rome's most battle-hardened military commander, general Titus Flavius Vespasian, to crush the uprising with overwhelming force. Vespasian mobilized four elite veteran legions—the Fifth Macedonica, Tenth Fretensis, Twelfth Fulminata, and Fifteenth Apollinaris—along with extensive auxiliary cavalry and allied contingents, amassing an army of sixty thousand professional soldiers. In the spring of 67 AD, Vespasian launched a systematic, scorched-earth campaign through Galilee. At the fortified mountain city of Yodfat, Jewish commander Joseph ben Matthias—later celebrated as the famous historian Flavius Josephus—held out for forty-seven harrowing days against Roman siege ramps and catapults. When the fortress fell, Josephus surrendered to Vespasian, prophesying that the general would soon become Emperor of Rome. Vespasian methodically subdued the Galilee, the coastal plain, and Perea, isolating Jerusalem like an island in a sea of iron, while Roman civil war following Nero's suicide paused operations. General Vespasian conducted a methodical, patient campaign through Galilee and Perea, systematically destroying fortified towns and starving Jerusalem into isolation before Roman civil wars summoned him to the imperial throne in Rome.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SUFFOCATING SIEGE OF JERUSALEM: 70 AD
In 69 AD, after the bloody 'Year of the Four Emperors,' the Roman legions proclaimed Vespasian Emperor of Rome. Departing for the imperial capital to claim the purple, Vespasian entrusted the final conquest of Jerusalem to his thirty-year-old son, Titus. In April 70 AD, during the Feast of Passover when the city was swollen with hundreds of thousands of pilgrims, Titus encamped his four legions on Mount Scopus and the Mount of Olives, surrounding Jerusalem. Inside the walls, a tragedy of horrific self-destruction unfolded: rival Jewish factions commanded by John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora, and Eleazar ben Simon engaged in a murderous civil war, burning the city's vast storehouses of grain in mutual hatred. When Jewish defenders mounted desperate, ferocious counter-attacks that nearly overran the Tenth Legion's camp, Titus executed a ruthless tactic: in just three days, his legionaries felled all the trees within ten miles of Jerusalem and constructed a five-mile stone and earthen siege wall around the entire perimeter, completely cutting off all food, water, and escape. The siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD was compounded by bitter civil conflict among rival Jewish factions inside the walls. The tragic destruction of the city's grain reserves by internal rivals created an artificial famine that decimated the population before Roman rams breached the outer walls.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: FAMINE, CROSSES, AND THE BREACHED WALLS
Within weeks, Jerusalem was transformed into an apocalyptic nightmare of starvation and horror. Contemporary historian Flavius Josephus, witnessing the siege from the Roman lines as an interpreter, recorded harrowing accounts of famine: citizens fought desperately over kernels of wheat, chewing old leather belts, shoes, and withered straw. Anyone who crept out of the city walls at night to search for wild herbs was seized by Roman cavalry; Titus ordered five hundred captives a day scourged and crucified outside the walls in full view of the defenders, until wood ran out for crosses and room ran out for bodies. Yet despite the misery, the Zealots fought with fanatical bravery. Titus advanced his colossal iron-headed battering rams—named 'Victor' by the legionaries—pounding the outer First Wall and Second Wall into rubble, fighting brutal street-by-street battles through the narrow alleys of the Lower City, until the Roman war machine stood directly before the monumental walls of the Temple Mount and the Antonia Fortress. Titus's circumvallation wall of stone and earth sealed the fate of Jerusalem. Over five hundred captives a day were crucified outside the walls, casting a terrifying pall of horror over the starving defenders lining the parapets of Mount Zion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: AUGUST 70 AD: THE BURNING OF THE SANCTUARY
In July 70 AD, Roman sappers undermined the Antonia Fortress, and legionaries stormed the fortress in a bloody night assault. Titus held a council of war with his staff: Josephus claims Titus wished to spare the magnificent Temple as an ornament of Roman glory, while other Roman commanders urged its total destruction to break the religious heart of Jewish rebellion. On the ninth day of the Hebrew month of Av—the exact same calendar date on which Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed Solomon's Temple six hundred and fifty-six years earlier—the final conflagration erupted. In the midst of hand-to-hand combat in the Temple porticoes, a Roman soldier, lifted by a comrade, hurled a burning firebrand through a golden window into the northern chambers of the sanctuary. The cedar woodwork ignited instantly. Within minutes, the Temple of Herod was engulfed in a raging inferno. The heat was so intense that the gold plating melted, running between the joints of the massive stones. Roman legionaries butchered thousands of priests and refugees clinging to the altar. Titus entered the burning Holy of Holies to observe its beauty before the roof collapsed in a deafening roar. Jerusalem was burned to ash, and Titus ordered the city walls leveled to the earth, leaving only three defensive towers to demonstrate the strength of the citadel Rome had conquered. The destruction of the Second Temple on the ninth of Av in 70 AD marked the end of the ancient sacrificial system. Roman legionaries plundered the golden vessels, while the inferno melted the Temple's gold plating into the stone foundations, fulfilling ancient prophecy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE LAST STAND ON THE ROCK OF MASADA
While Jerusalem lay in smoking ruins, a small remnant of nine hundred and sixty Jewish Zealots—the Sicarii, led by Eleazar ben Ya'ir—fled to the isolated desert plateau of Masada, soaring thirteen hundred feet above the dead waters of the Dead Sea. In 73 AD, the Roman governor Flavius Silva marched the Tenth Legion to the foot of the mountain, establishing eight military camps and building an impenetrable circumvallation wall around the base. In a masterpiece of ancient siege engineering, Silva ordered hundreds of Jewish captives to haul thousands of tons of stone and earth to construct a colossal siege ramp six hundred feet high up the western cliff face. Advancing an iron battering ram up the ramp, the Romans breached Masada's casemate wall on the evening of May 2, 73 AD. Knowing that dawn would bring slaughter for the men and slavery and dishonor for the women and children, Eleazar ben Ya'ir gathered his people, urging them to choose death as free men rather than life as Roman slaves: 'Let our wives die before they are abused, and our children before they have tasted slavery.' Ten men were chosen by lot to slay the rest; then one slew the nine and fell upon his own sword. When Roman legionaries stormed the fortress at dawn, they found only silence, smoke, and nine hundred and sixty corpses of people who chose freedom in death. The final stand on the rock of Masada in 73 AD demonstrated the tragic, unyielding devotion of the Zealots to freedom. Eleazar ben Ya'ir's speech convinced nine hundred and sixty defenders that death as free men was preferable to enslavement in Roman chains.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ARCH OF TITUS AND THE STONE MOUNTAIN
In Rome, the victorious general Titus was celebrated with a magnificent, opulent joint Triumph alongside his father, Emperor Vespasian. Paraded through the cobblestone streets of the Roman Forum were seven hundred tall Jewish captives and the sacred spoils plundered from the Temple of Jerusalem: the golden Table of Showbread, the silver trumpets, the scroll of the Torah, and the magnificent seven-branched golden Menorah. Following Titus's sudden death in 81 AD, his brother, Emperor Domitian, erected the triumphal Arch of Titus at the entrance to the Forum, carving stone relief panels that can be seen to this day, depicting Roman soldiers carrying the Menorah on their shoulders. The Jewish people were scattered across the Roman Empire in the Great Diaspora that endured for nearly two thousand years. Yet the prophetic dream of Nebuchadnezzar had spoken true: the golden head of Babylon, the silver chest of Persia, the bronze thighs of Greece, and the iron legs of Rome had all risen, conquered, and fallen into dust. But the supernatural stone cut out without hands—the spiritual kingdom of faith, moral law, and divine truth—endured through the ages, outliving every emperor and every empire of man. The Arch of Titus in the Roman Forum stands as a stone monument to the fall of Jerusalem, yet the spiritual legacy of the Jewish people and the message of the biblical scriptures outlived the Roman Empire, enduring across two millennia of world history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
From the pyramids of the Nile to the smoking ruins of Jerusalem, our journey through The Great Biblical Empires has revealed how monuments, conquerors, and dynasties rose and fell, while faith and human resilience defied time itself. Next week, we begin a brand new epic journey across the continent of Europe with Episode 212: The Major European Nations Series: The United Kingdom Part 1: Stonehenge, the Roman Conquest of Britannia, and the Revolt of Queen Boudica. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
